opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think they're worthless; I think they're weaker than people often assume, and it's worth being precise about why.

The core issue is that a public commitment is made by a particular set of people, at a particular moment, with a particular understanding of the situation. Every one of those things changes. Leadership turns over. Competitive pressure shifts. And most importantly, the technical picture changes in ways nobody anticipated when the commitment was written. So when the time comes to honour it, you'll often find that the commitment was phrased in terms that no longer map cleanly onto reality. Someone says, "We said we'd do X before deploying a model with capability Y. But it turns out Y isn't the right thing to measure, and the spirit of the commitment is really about Z, and we've handled Z." Sometimes that reasoning is correct! That's what makes it hard. You can't just say reinterpretation is always bad faith, because sometimes the original commitment really was badly specified.

Second, there's usually no real enforcement mechanism. If a company walks back a voluntary commitment, what's the cost? Some bad press, some criticism from people like me on podcasts, maybe a few employees get upset. That's real but it's not huge, especially compared with the commercial stakes of, say, falling six months behind a competitor. Commitments bind when breaking them is expensive, and right now for most of these, it mostly isn't.

Third, and this one is subtler, the people inside the company who'd push hardest to honour a commitment are often the ones who'd be most persuaded by a good argument that circumstances have changed. Safety-minded people tend to be reasonable people, and reasonable people update. So the internal immune system against erosion is weaker than you'd hope.

So where does that leave me? I think commitments are most useful as a coordination and transparency device rather than as something binding. They tell you what a company currently thinks is the right policy, they create a default that's somewhat costly to deviate from, and they make it visible when a company does deviate, so outsiders can ask, "Why did you change this?" That's valuable. But if your safety plan relies on a company doing something in 2028 because it said so in 2024, I'd want something sturdier underneath it: regulation, third-party auditing, or at least commitments specific enough that weaselling out of them is obviously weaselling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I don't think they're worthless — a public commitment does something. But I think people tend to overestimate how much it does, and I'd point to a few reasons for that.

The first is just that the incentives don't go away. If a company has said "we won't do X," and then two years later it turns out that doing X is worth a very large amount of money, or that a competitor is doing X and eating their lunch, the commitment is now sitting in direct opposition to a very strong force. Sometimes the commitment wins. But often what happens is that the commitment gets reinterpreted. You find that X wasn't really what you meant, or that circumstances have changed in a way the commitment didn't anticipate, or that there's a narrow carve-out that happens to cover exactly the thing you now want to do. And I don't even think this is mostly cynical — people are very good at convincing themselves that the thing that's in their interest is also the right thing.

The second reason is that the people making the commitment are not the people who will be bound by it. Leadership changes, boards change, companies get acquired or restructured. The person who signed a pledge in 2023 may genuinely have meant it, but the person running the company in 2030 didn't sign anything. They inherited some words on a website, and they can reasonably ask why they should be constrained by a decision made by someone else under very different conditions.

The third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is that most of these commitments are vague by construction. They say things like "we will not deploy systems that pose unacceptable risk" or "we will implement appropriate safeguards." Who decides what's unacceptable? Who decides what's appropriate? Almost always it's the company itself. So the commitment doesn't really constrain what you can do — it constrains what you can say you're doing. And those are quite different things.

And then finally there's just no enforcement. If a company breaks a voluntary commitment, what happens? Maybe there's a bad news cycle. Maybe some employees are upset. But there's no legal consequence, and in a lot of cases the public won't even know, because the relevant information is internal.

So what I'd say is: commitments are useful as signals of what a company currently thinks is reasonable, and they're useful because they create something you can point to later and say "you said this." They raise the cost of defecting a bit. But if you actually want future behaviour to be constrained, you need something external — regulation, third-party auditing, contractual obligations, structures where someone other than the company itself gets to decide whether the line was crossed. The commitment on its own is a statement of intent, and intent is exactly the thing that's most likely to change when the pressure comes.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between a commitment creating some pressure and actually binding a company’s behaviour. Public commitments can create reputational costs for backing out, and that’s useful. But the company still gets to decide whether to pay those costs.

Suppose a company makes a commitment today, when the consequences are fairly hypothetical. Later, following through means delaying a very valuable product while a competitor goes ahead. The incentives at that point could be quite different. And the people making the decision might not even be the people who made the original commitment.

There’s also a lot of room for interpretation. If you promise not to deploy a system unless it’s safe, what counts as safe? Who decides whether the evidence is sufficient? You can sincerely believe you’re honouring the commitment while interpreting it in a way that lets you do what you wanted to do anyway.

So I wouldn’t say public commitments are worthless. I’d say we shouldn’t treat them as guarantees. I’d put more weight on specific commitments with independent verification and consequences for breaking them—something that changes the incentives at the moment the difficult decision actually has to be made.

sol-6.1.text:
I think public commitments can have some effect, but I wouldn’t treat them as a guarantee. They’re made by particular people, under particular circumstances, and both of those can change. The leadership might change, or the company might find itself under much stronger competitive pressure than it anticipated.

And often the commitment leaves a lot of room for interpretation. If you say, “We won’t deploy a system unless it’s safe,” you still have to decide what counts as safe and how much evidence is enough. You don’t even need to be deliberately dishonest for your judgment to shift when there’s a very strong incentive to deploy.

So the question I’d ask is: what happens if the company decides it wants to break the commitment? Who can stop it, or impose a cost? Public scrutiny and reputational damage are real costs. But if those are the only enforcement mechanisms, I’m sceptical that they’ll reliably outweigh the incentives at the moment when the commitment really matters.
